name: Palenque
info: Palenque was a Maya city-state near the Usumacinta River in Chiapas, southern Mexico, occupied from about 226 BCE to about 799 CE, and best known for the reign of Kʼinich Janaabʼ Pakal and his tomb.

facts.founded: The ruins date from about 226 BCE; the first king of the city-state known by name, Kʼuk Balam, began to rule in 431, and he is supposed to have founded the dynasty.
facts.where: Near the Usumacinta River in the Mexican state of Chiapas, about 130 km south of Ciudad del Carmen and 150 metres above sea level, beside the modern town of Palenque.
facts.known: The reign of Kʼinich Janaabʼ Pakal (615 to 683); his tomb in the Temple of the Inscriptions; the Palace; the Temples of the Cross group; hieroglyphic inscriptions; the sacks of 599, 611 and 711; its aqueducts
facts.today: Palenque is an excavated and restored archaeological site in Chiapas, protected since 1981 as Palenque National Park.

t: Palenque was a Maya city-state whose known dynasty began with Kʼuk Balam in 431, and which was sacked by Calakmul and its client states in 599 and 611 before it recovered.
Kʼinich Janaabʼ Pakal ruled from 615 to 683 and, with his sons, built most of the palaces and temples that stand today; the city was sacked again by Toniná in 711.

Elite building at the ceremonial centre ended some time after 800, farmers stayed for a few generations, and the forest then grew over the site, which was visited, drawn and excavated by outsiders from 1773 onwards.
dyk: Pakal's tomb was entered in 1952 by Alberto Ruz Lhuillier, the first person to look on it in over a thousand years, after four years of work at the Temple of the Inscriptions; a jade mosaic mask lay over the king's face.
ev: The date from which the ruins of Palenque are dated
Kʼuk Balam begins to rule as the first known king of the city-state
Troops from Calakmul invade and sack Palenque
Kʼinich Janaabʼ Pakal begins his reign of nearly seventy years
Pakal dies and his son Kʼinich Kan Bʼalam becomes king
Toniná sacks Palenque and takes Kʼinich Kʼan Joy Chitam II prisoner
Elite building at the ceremonial centre comes to an end
Alberto Ruz Lhuillier opens the passage to Pakal's tomb

sections.origins:
Palenque stands near the Usumacinta River in the Mexican state of Chiapas, about 130 km south of Ciudad del Carmen and 150 metres above sea level, beside the modern town of Palenque. The climate is humid, averaging 26 °C with roughly 2,160 millimetres of rain a year. Its ancient name in the Itzaʼ language was Lakamha, meaning "big water" or "big waters", a name that suits a site of steep limestone hills, active springs and heavy rainfall. In Yucatec Maya it is called Bàakʼ, and the city-state is also called Bʼaakal. The ruins date from about 226 BCE to about 799 CE.

The early history is complex. Mythological beings appear in the titles of the kings, with a variety of emblem glyphs, and Kʼukʼ Bahlam I, the supposed founder of the dynasty, is called a Toktan Ajaw in the text of the Temple of the Foliated Cross. A list of possible and known rulers names figures as early as about 2325 BCE, but the first ajaw of Bʼaakal known to us was Kʼuk Balam, "Quetzal Jaguar", who governed for four years from 431. After him came a king whom archaeologists nicknamed "Casper", and the next two kings were probably his sons. Little was known of the first of them, Bʼutz Aj Sak Chiik, until 1994, when a tablet describing a ritual for the king was found.
sections.growth:
The first king to reach great prestige was Ahkal Moʼ Naab I, who died in 524; the kings who followed him were proud to be his descendants. His successor Kʼan Joy Chitam I governed for 36 years from 529. The sons of Kʼan Joy Chitam I, Ahkal Moʼ Naab II and Kʼan Bʼalam I, were the first kings to use the title Kinich, "the great sun", which later kings also used.

The buildings that stand today probably represent a rebuilding after the attacks of 599 and 611. Kʼinich Janaabʼ Pakal, who ruled from 615 to 683, is credited as one of the main figures behind the rebuilding and a renaissance in the city's art and architecture. Most of the palaces and temples of Palenque were built during his government, and the city flourished as never before, eclipsing Tikal. The central complex known as the Palace was enlarged and remodelled several times, notably in 654, 661 and 668. A text in the Palace describes Palenque as newly allied with Tikal and with Yaxchilan, and says that they captured the six enemy kings of the opposing alliance.

His son Kʼinich Kan Bʼalam continued the architectural and sculptural works and began several projects of his own, including the Group of the Crosses. His brother and successor, Kʼinich Kʼan Joy Chitam II, rebuilt and enlarged the northern side of the Palace. The reigns of these three kings were a century of expansion. By 2005 the area uncovered covered up to 2.5 square kilometres, and it is estimated that less than a tenth of the city has been explored.
sections.rulers:
The dynasty of Palenque is known from the hieroglyphic inscriptions. After Kʼuk Balam (431) and "Casper" came Bʼutz Aj Sak Chiik, Ahkal Moʼ Nahb I (501 to 524) and Kʼan Joy Chitam I (529 to 565). Kan Bahlam I (572 to 583) was succeeded in 583 by Yohl Ikʼnal, who was supposedly his daughter.

Troops from Calakmul sacked Palenque in 599, under Yohl Ikʼnal, a military feat without known precedent. A second victory by Calakmul came about twelve years later, in 611, under her son Aj Neʼ Yohl Mat, when the king of Calakmul entered Palenque in person. Aj Neʼ Yohl Mat died in 612, and a period of political disorder followed. It is believed that Janaab Pakal, also called Pakal I, then took power by a political agreement; he exercised the functions of the ajaw but was never crowned. He was succeeded in 612 by his daughter, Sak Kʼukʼ, who governed for three years until her son was old enough to rule. That son, Kʼinich Janaabʼ Pakal, Pakal the Great, began to rule at the age of twelve in 615. His mother remained an important force for the first 25 years of his rule and may have ruled jointly with him.

Pakal reigned until 683. His older son Kʼinich Kan Bʼalam took the kingship, and in 702 he was succeeded by his brother Kʼinich Kʼan Joy Chitam II. After Palenque was sacked by Toniná in 711 and the old king was taken prisoner, there was no king for ten years. Kʼinich Ahkal Moʼ Nabʼ III was crowned in 722. There is no evidence that he was the direct heir of the captured king, so his coronation is believed to mark a break in the dynastic line. He, his son and his grandson governed until the end of the 8th century.
sections.life:
The Palace was used by the Maya aristocracy for bureaucratic functions, entertainment and ritual ceremonies. It stands in the centre of the ancient city on a wide artificial terrace, and several generations built it over a period of four centuries. It is a complex of connected and adjacent buildings and courtyards, the largest in Palenque, measuring 97 metres by 73 metres at its base. Its most recognisable feature is a four-storey tower called the Observation Tower. The Palace had numerous large baths and saunas, supplied with fresh water by an intricate water system. An aqueduct with a three-metre-high vault diverted the Otulum River to flow underneath the main plaza.

Other structures included temples, tombs, elite residences, a court for the Mesoamerican ballgame and a stone bridge over the Otulum River. Archaeologists identified the Piedras Bolas aqueduct as a pressurised aqueduct, the earliest known in the New World: a spring-fed conduit on steep ground with a restricted outlet, from which water would have jetted to a height of 6 metres. Its use is not known.

The people of Palenque also collected fossils. The limestone slabs used to build the temples, and the quarries they came from, hold well-preserved marine fossils of the Early Paleocene. The Maya residents appear to have known of them and to have collected them, using fossil shark teeth and ray spines as cutting tools, painting some of the fish skeletons and cutting slabs to display the fossils better. Women could rule: Sak Kʼukʼ governed from 612, though female rulers were shown with male attributes.
sections.crises:
Palenque suffered three great defeats. In 599 troops from Calakmul invaded and sacked the city under Yohl Ikʼnal, and in 611 the king of Calakmul entered it in person. The glyphic panels of the Temple of the Inscriptions say that some fundamental annual ceremonies were not held in 613 and state: "Lost is the divine lady, lost is the king." No mention of the government of that time has been found. The city was at a low point when Pakal came to power in 615.

In 711 the realm of Toniná sacked Palenque and took the old king Kʼinich Kʼan Joy Chitam II prisoner. His final fate is not known, and it is presumed that he was executed at Toniná. The war with Toniná continued after the coronation of Kʼinich Ahkal Moʼ Nabʼ III, and inscriptions record a new defeat of Palenque.

During the 8th century Bʼaakal came under increasing stress, as did most other Classic Maya city-states, and there was no new elite construction in the ceremonial centre some time after 800. An agricultural population continued to live there for a few generations. Then the site was abandoned, and the forest slowly grew over it. The district was very sparsely populated when the Spanish first arrived in the 1520s.
sections.legacy:
The Temple of the Inscriptions began perhaps as early as 675 as the funerary monument of Pakal. Its superstructure holds the second longest glyphic text known from the Maya world and records about 180 years of the city's history. In 1952 Alberto Ruz Lhuillier lifted a stone slab in the floor of the back room and found a passage, filled in shortly before the abandonment, that led down a long stairway to the tomb. It held a large carved sarcophagus, the richest collection of jade seen in a Maya tomb, a jade mosaic mask over the face and a suit of jade held together by gold wire. The tomb showed for the first time that such pyramids were also funerary structures.

The city is historically significant for its extensive hieroglyphic texts of the reigns of Pakal, his son Kʼinich Kan Bahlam II and his grandson Kʼinich Akal Moʼ Naabʼ. At Palenque Heinrich Berlin, and later Linda Schele and Peter Mathews, outlined the first dynastic list for any Maya city.

Outsiders came to the ruins from 1773: Ramon de Ordoñez y Aguilar, then Antonio del Río and Antonio Bernasconi, whose men damaged the Palace while Bernasconi made the first map. Juan Galindo visited in 1831 and noted that the figures in the art looked like the local Native Americans, though some early explorers attributed the site to Egyptians, Polynesians or the Lost Tribes of Israel. Waldeck, Stephens and Catherwood, Charnay and Maudslay followed. The site has since been excavated and restored, and Palenque National Park, designated in 1981, covers 17.72 square kilometres.

summary: Palenque was a Maya city-state near the Usumacinta River in Chiapas, whose ruins date from about 226 BCE to about 799 CE. Kʼinich Janaabʼ Pakal ruled it from 615 to 683 and built much of what stands today. It was abandoned and overgrown, then excavated and restored.
notes: START/END: the article dates the ruins 'ca. 226 BC to ca. 799 AD'; I used -226 and 799, both approximate. The first known king is 431.

Accession of Kʼinich Ahkal Moʼ Nabʼ III: the prose says crowned in 722, the ruler list says 721; I used 722 from the prose. Pakal II and III and Kan Bahlam III (c. 742, c. 751, 764 to c. 783, 799) are in the list only, so the later reigns are not narrated beyond 'until the end of the 8th century'.

Janaab Pakal (Pakal I): the prose says he took power after Aj Neʼ Yohl Mat's death and was succeeded in 612 by his daughter; the list gives 'c. 612, position uncertain'. Sak Kʼukʼ is given as ruling 'only three years' and 'at least three years starting in 612'; the same sentence of the article says she 'resigned' in favour of her son; I wrote that she governed until he was old enough.

Ahkal Moʼ Naab I: the list gives 501 to 524, the Temple text 'Ahkal Moʼ Nahb I'; spellings vary across the article (Kan Bahlam, Kʼan Bʼalam, Kinich/Kʼinich) and I kept the variants as the article spells them where I quoted a list.
The article says Kan Bʼalam 'finished the construction of the famous tomb', and says the Temple of the Inscriptions 'began perhaps as early as 675'; I gave the 675 hedge only.

The article calls Kʼan Bʼalam I's successor sequence confusing: 'Kʼan Bʼalam I' (572 to 583) and Kʼinich Kan Bʼalam (Kan Bahlam II, 684 to 702) are different kings; the article's own text also writes 'Kʼinich Kan Bʼalam I' for the Group of the Crosses builder. I called him Kʼinich Kan Bʼalam, Pakal's older son, without a number.

Left out: the article's claim that Palenque 'perished in the 8th century' beside its own date of c. 799 and building until 'sometime after 800' (kept 799 and 'some time after 800'); the exact visitor figure of 2017 (tourism); the paleontological dating details; the Pakal sarcophagus lid iconography; the June 2022 stucco head find; Piedras Bolas discovery credits (Duffy and French, 2010); details of the Cross group reliefs.

'Eclipsing Tikal' and 'flourished as never before' are the article's own claims about Pakal's reign; the Palace text on the alliance with Tikal and Yaxchilan is given as 'not much more had been translated'. The Palace construction dates (654, 661, 668) are as stated.
The article's statement that the 'psychoduct' of the tomb and the winter-solstice alignment are suggestions was left out for space. The site has 'less than 10%' explored; I wrote 'less than a tenth'.

Who first reached the site: the article says only that the Spanish found the district sparsely populated in the 1520s and mentions 'de la Nada's brief account' without a date or first name; I did not name him. The Maya people of the region never lost knowledge of the site according to nothing in the article either way, so nothing is claimed; no 'discovery' wording is used.
'Lost is the divine lady, lost is the king' is a quotation from the article. 'Women could rule' is from the article's statement that city-state lords were occasionally women.
